A cruet is a small container designed specifically for holding and pouring liquid condiments or seasonings at the dining table.

Think about sitting down for a meal and wanting to drizzle some olive oil on your salad, or splash a little vinegar on your fish and chips. The small, narrow bottle or jar that holds that oil or vinegar — the one you pour from — that's a cruet.

It is not a regular bottle, not a bowl, and not a jar in the everyday sense. It is specifically a table vessel — small enough to pass around, designed with a narrow opening so you can pour or sprinkle with control, and often fitted with a stopper (a small cap or plug) to keep the contents fresh and prevent spills.

A cruet is typically:

  • Small — easily held in one hand
  • Made of glass, ceramic, or metal
  • Narrow-necked, allowing controlled pouring
  • Sometimes fitted with a stopper or cork at the top
  • Occasionally with a small handle or spout

The design is deliberately elegant and functional — it suits the table setting without looking out of place beside plates and cutlery.

Traditionally, cruets hold liquid condiments and seasonings, such as:

  • Vinegar (very classically associated with cruets)
  • Oil (olive oil, for example)
  • Soy sauce
  • Hot sauce or chili sauce
  • Sometimes even salt water solutions (liquid seasonings)

Salt and pepper, when they come in matching small vessels of the same set, are sometimes loosely called cruets too, though strictly speaking those are shakers. In common, relaxed usage, the word can stretch to include them.

You will very often hear the word used in the phrase "cruet set" or "cruet stand." This refers to a matched group of small condiment containers arranged together on a small tray or frame for the table.

A classic cruet set typically contains:

  • An oil bottle
  • A vinegar bottle
  • Salt and pepper holders

They sit together on a little stand or tray, looking neat and uniform, and are passed around the table during a meal. You'll find cruet sets on dining tables in homes, and very commonly in restaurants — particularly in older, traditional, or formal dining settings.

The word also has a distinct, specific meaning in the context of Christian religious ceremonies — particularly in Catholic, Anglican, and other liturgical church traditions.

In this context, a cruet is one of a pair of small vessels (usually made of glass or precious metal) used during the Mass or Eucharist service. One cruet holds wine, and the other holds water. These are used by the priest when preparing the Communion cup on the altar.

So if you encounter the word in a religious or church-related text, it refers to these sacred ceremonial containers — not the ones on your dinner table. The shape and purpose (small, narrow, for pouring a liquid) remain the same, but the context shifts entirely to worship.

Here are a few examples to help anchor the word:

  • "She poured a few drops of balsamic vinegar from the cruet onto her salad."
  • "The waiter placed a cruet set on the table, containing oil, vinegar, salt, and pepper."
  • "The altar server carried the cruets of wine and water to the priest."
  • "The antique silver cruet had a delicate stopper and a tiny handle."

A cruet is defined by three qualities working together:

  1. It is small.
  2. It is meant to hold a pourable liquid (a condiment or a ceremonial liquid).
  3. It lives on a table — either a dining table or an altar.

It's a word with a pleasantly specific and narrow meaning. When someone says "cruet," they are almost always pointing to one of two things: the little bottle on your dinner table holding oil or vinegar, or the sacred vessel in a church holding wine or water. The word never wanders far from these two uses.
